content: The Sumatran Pine, scientifically known as Pinus merkusii, is a species of pine tree native to Southeast Asia. Its primary distribution is in the mountainous regions of northern Sumatra, with additional populations found on Mount Kerinci and Mount Talang in central Sumatra. Outside of Sumatra, it is also found in the Philippines, specifically on the island of Mindoro and in the Zambales Mountains of western Luzon. The population of Pinus merkusii in central Sumatra, located between 1°40' and 2°06' south latitude, represents the only naturally occurring pine species found south of the Equator. This tree typically grows at moderate altitudes, ranging from 400 to 1500 meters above sea level, although it can occasionally be found as low as 90 meters and as high as 2000 meters. The Sumatran Pine is a medium-sized to large tree, capable of reaching heights of 25 to 45 meters, with a trunk diameter of up to 1 meter. Its bark is orange-red in color, thick and deeply fissured at the base of the trunk, while becoming thinner and flaky in the upper crown. The leaves, commonly referred to as needles, are arranged in pairs. They are very slender, measuring 15 to 20 centimeters in length and less than 1 millimeter in thickness, with a coloration that ranges from green to yellowish-green. The cones of the Sumatran Pine are narrow and conical in shape, measuring 5 to 8 centimeters in length and approximately 2 centimeters in width at the base when closed. Initially green, the cones mature to a glossy red-brown color. Upon reaching maturity, the cones open to a width of 4 to 5 centimeters to release seeds. The seeds themselves are 5 to 6 millimeters long and are equipped with a wing measuring 15 to 20 millimeters, facilitating wind dispersal. This species is closely related to the Tenasserim Pine (Pinus latteri), which is found further north in Southeast Asia, from Myanmar to Vietnam. Some botanists consider the two species to be conspecific, grouping them under the name Pinus merkusii, as it was described first. However, the Tenasserim Pine differs in having longer (18 to 27 centimeters) and thicker (over 1 millimeter) needles, as well as larger cones with thicker scales. Additionally, the cones of the Tenasserim Pine often remain closed for an extended period after reaching maturity. The Sumatran Pine also shares similarities with a group of Mediterranean pines, including the Aleppo Pine (Pinus halepensis) and the Turkish Pine (Pinus brutia), as they exhibit several overlapping characteristics.
